question: to the Commission Gerald Hauser (PfE) Subject:
mRNA COVID-19 vaccines in Europe: transparency in batch testing and adverse reaction reports

Several reports suggest considerable variation in adverse reactions to individual batches of mRNA vaccines. Here are two examples: Schmeling, Manniche and Hansen (2023), ‘Batch-dependent safety of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 vaccine’, Journal: European Journal of Clinical Investigation1. The authors analysed Danish reporting data on Pfizer/BioNTech (BNT162b2) and found that the number of suspected cases of adverse events varied considerably between batches. They described clusters of batches with different rates of reporting and identified these as a ‘batch‑dependent safety signal’. The authors called for further study on the matter. – Manniche et al. (2024), ‘Reports of Batch-Dependent Suspected Adverse Events of the BNT162b2 mRNA COVID-19 Vaccine: Comparison of Results from Denmark and Sweden’, Journal: Medicines2. This study compared suspected cases in Denmark and Sweden. The authors reported that similar patterns of variation between batches had been observed in both countries. They stressed that the results were preliminary and hypothesis-generating. 1.
Does the Commission know what independent assessments have been carried out on individual batches of mRNA vaccines, and what conclusion was drawn?
Does the Commission know what variation has been observed between batches of mRNA vaccines in quality controls, and is there also variation between EU Member States?
Has the Commission launched investigations into published observations regarding variations in adverse reaction reports between batches?

answer: EN on behalf of the European Commission (22.7.2026) Once a COVID-19 vaccine has received approval, each batch can only be released following quality control testing to confirm that the product is in line with the specifications approved as part of the marketing authorisation. For most centrally authorised vaccines, an additional independent control is performed by a Member State Official Medicines Control Laboratory before their release in the EU. The Commission also refers the Honourable Member to the reply to parliamentary question (PQ) E-001537/20231, where this point was addressed. Only batches complying with the approved quality specifications can be released. The Commission does not hold comparative batch-level quality control data by Member State. However, the European Medicines Agency (EMA) has no evidence suggesting that some batches of COVID-19 vaccines caused more, or more serious, side effects than other batches. For Comirnaty, this was already indicated in the reply to PQ P-002990/20242. Furthermore, pharmacovigilance systems are in place to monitor the suspected adverse reactions and detect safety issues potentially related to quality. The EMA and national authorities continuously monitor safety, including EudraVigilance reports, medical literature and product quality issue detection tools3. Analyses performed by the EMA of suspected cases of adverse reactions did not reveal an increased risk of side effects for specific batches. This was also indicated in the answer to PQ E-001537/2023.
